analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a Senate committee and sat on the Senate calendar for 18 months without ever reaching a floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required most employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven days) a year, for their own illness, a family member's care, doctor visits, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Smaller employers would have to provide the same 56 hours but could leave it unpaid. It also covered federal workers, congressional staff, rail carriers, the Government Accountability Office, and the Library of Congress, and it barred employers from firing or punishing workers who used the time.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who currently have no paid sick leave, and their families: they could stay home with the flu, take a child to the doctor, or attend court after an assault without losing pay or their job. The bill's sponsors and outside estimates put the number of workers without any paid sick time in the tens of millions, concentrated in low-wage service jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with no paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness, preventive care, care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or chosen family, and for medical, relocation, or legal needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Employers with fewer than 15 employees may opt out of paying for the time but must still provide 56 hours of unpaid sick leave each year under the same rules.

The bill makes it unlawful to fire, retaliate against, or count sick days against a worker in no-fault attendance policies, and it gives the Labor Department investigative and enforcement powers, plus a private right of action with attorney's fees and liquidated damages.

It covers federal employees, congressional employing offices, Government Accountability Office and Library of Congress staff, and rail carriers, and it does not preempt state or local laws with more generous sick leave.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more workers — especially retail, food service, hospitality, and other low-wage, high-turnover industries — bear the cost of paid time off, record-keeping, and notices; the general public would face no direct cost since the bill authorizes no new federal spending beyond outreach.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for employers, and the heaviest relative burden falls on small businesses and low-margin, high-turnover industries where workers are least likely to already have paid sick leave.

Employers with fewer than 15 employees get no paid-leave requirement at all — only unpaid leave — and businesses with existing paid leave policies that meet the bill's standards owe nothing extra, so coverage is not universal.

The entitlement is modest: 56 hours a year, no payout of unused time when a worker leaves, and workers must generally wait 60 days after hire and make a reasonable effort to schedule leave so it does not disrupt operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without paid sick leave, seven days a year to recover from illness or care for family without losing wages or a job is a substantial, concrete benefit, and opponents' strongest argument — that it raises labor costs — is real but is the same cost every existing state and local paid sick leave law has imposed. The bill is conservatively designed: existing generous policies are exempt, small employers can pay nothing, unused time need not be cashed out, and scheduling flexibility protects operations.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar of business in July 2023, but it was never scheduled for a floor vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 17, 2023, with 42 original cosponsors including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and Health Committee Chair Patty Murray.
All 42 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on.

The Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on June 21, 2023, and Senator Sanders formally reported it without amendment on July 18, 2023.
That same day the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 136) — a step that means it was cleared by committee and waiting for floor time.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a floor vote, never reached the House, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly industries that do not currently provide paid sick leave — are better off, because they avoided the mandate; workers without sick leave gained nothing, though many states and cities kept or added their own laws. The 42 cosponsors had cleared the bill through committee, but the Senate leadership never allotted floor time to it, and no Republican supported it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared the mandate; sick workers gained nothing

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (I-VT), bill sponsor and committee reporter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, recruited 42 cosponsors, and reported it out of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without amendment.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Her committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment in June 2023.

for.name: 42 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, giving the bill enough signatures to fill a committee calendar but not a floor majority of 60.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but, as the senator who decides what reaches the floor, never scheduled it for a vote during the 18 months it sat on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsorship and no support for the bill at any point in the 118th Congress.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal paid-sick-leave mandates, arguing they raise labor costs for employers, especially small businesses.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats or an independent aligned with them; not a single Republican senator signed on, and the bill never came to a floor vote where party splits could be counted.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These low-wage, high-turnover industries would bear the largest new cost of providing paid sick time, since their workers are the least likely to already have it — and that cost is precisely the wage security the bill gives their employees.
Exempt from paying, but must still track and grant 56 hours of unpaid leave with the same notice, certification, and anti-retaliation rules, a compliance burden without a wage cost.

Rail carriers are expressly covered, including train crews, maintenance-of-way, and dispatch workers — a population whose lack of sick days was a live national issue — and would owe paid sick time to those crafts.

industries.industry: Federal government and congressional employing offices
industries.note: Congress, the GAO, the Library of Congress, and executive agencies are covered, meaning the bill applied its own mandate to the officeholders voting on it.
